comments.body: This analysis is a bit absurd.  It includes in its premise that the debate about affordability is due to near term inflation that has been recently experienced.  Sure, that exists but the frank reality is that when I discuss it among my peers it is that huge structural things have shifted.  The cost of homes, education and medical care all can grow and change over time in ways that are disconnected to what we earn.  My kid will face a 20’s with more debt as he becomes an adult when I did and a basic home in our area will be a factor of 2 or 3 times more than his expected starting income than I faced. As an older person, I’m looking at a medical world where there is no coherence in what things cost and there is no reasonable way for me to navigate/mitigate those expenses.  The layers of players in the middle who jack up drug prices and an impossible insurance bureaucracy make me feel incapable of “shopping” by price or negotiating my medical expenses.   These are long term structural changes that make our world feel less affordable than when we were young and fear for what our kids are inheriting.  This doesn’t even touch on the mountain of government debt that will come due some day as well.  It all leads to one phrase.  Eat the rich.

comments.name: CastleMan

Writing is a fundamental and vital skill. And, judging by the obvious decay in basic skills, Americans are rapidly losing the ability to do it. This trend threatens our ability to communicate with each other.

Schools need to ban all forms of technology in the classroom. And all written assignments must be done by handwriting only and in class. Otherwise, you can be sure that students will use AI.

But that won't be enough. Writing is a form of thinking, a way to make sense of new information, and a tool for learning in addition to a mode of expression. So it must be integrated into every subject in every classroom. 

Kids must again be taught how to build sentences, how to distinguish between verbs and nouns and adjectives and other forms, and, yes, how to spell. And we must hold them to a grade-appropriate standard that moves away from the "writing does not matter" ethos that has dominated our education system for 30 years or so.

comments.name: Jack
comments.body:
I have taught writing (composition) for over 50 years--high-school, university, overseas: even such career writing as technical, business, medical writing.  I am convinced that writing is the single-most  difficult task in any workplace.

It requires  language skills: grammar, diction, usage, etc.

It requires logic skills: beginning, middle end, and a multtiude of sidetracks.  Cause and effect. Deifnition of terms.

It requires audience: Who? When? Prior knowledge.  Teacher?  Colleague?  Boss?  President? 

Interpersonal skills : Purpose, persuasion?

It requires intrapersonal skills: voice, voices, personal growth, fear?

It requires an ear: What Do I sound like?  Is it me?   Can anyone read it aloud.  Should it be read aloud?

It requires a sense of space: What does it look like on paper, in a meme, on a tract or brochure?

And writing gives us a chance to put down our thoughts for a moment to re-read, reflect, and revise.  It hones our thoughts.

And we get to do this in a freshman composition course, or in a memo, or in an address to Congress.

Keep on writing people.

We are expecting too much if we expect the goal to be mitigated by anything resembling the constraints (most) humans put on themselves when trying to achieve a goal.  Yes, people cheat to get ahead, but the majority of us do not.  Most of us do not rob banks, for example, to fulfill the goal of getting more money.

So the answer to the question posed by the guest is simple: if you design a machine to do a task and it does not have the emotional intelligence to regulate itself and to accept that it might not be able to achieve that task without breaking the rules it should not break and that most humans are unwilling to break, then it will carry out the task by any means possible. comments.name: DJ
comments.body:
This topic opens the door to a much larger conversation, not only about teenage girls, but about our culture generally, perhaps women in particular: the universal need to be validated.

In a world of self-help, reality television, celebrity confession, views and likes, I've come to believe our idea of what validation means has become amplified and distorted. Being heard and understood is increasingly confused with having our feelings, interpretations and even our diagnoses affirmed by others.

I am a 58-year-old working and teaching artist and the daughter of a psychologist. I’ve joked that I’ve been “in therapy” all my life, and therapy language is very familiar to me. But the language of my mother’s profession, which peaked in the 70s–90s, feels very different from what began appearing among women with the rise of social media.

You'll hear it in yoga studios, art workshops and other spaces, often beginning when a teacher or leader folds a story of her own hardship or trauma into the instruction. The floodgates open: tell your “truth,” be witnessed, be validated, share the healing, pass it along.
It sounds and feels compassionate, but validation should not require agreement, and not every difficult experience needs to become trauma in order to deserve attention. Sometimes people simply came to learn yoga or make art. When participation begins to require adopting the emotional language of the group, it can feel less like community and a little more like landing in a cult.

comments.name: Jim Caruso
comments.body:
I have always believed that writing is thinking. It helps you clarify thoughts. As Ms. Stanger so eloquently says, “writing is a means to learning who you are and what you value,” and “Writing is thinking made visible: The sentence that resists you does so because the thought inside it is unfinished.”

For these reasons, I avoid using AI much in my writing, except for certain business applications, like compressing complexities into succinct bullet points for board meeting PowerPoints, and the assessment of tone in certain emails when I know the topic makes me angry or defensive.

But Ms. Stanger hasconvinced me that there’s a place for AI in creative writing too. In some ways it can be just a natural extension of the thesaurus function in Microsoft Word - helping to rephrase a sentence instead of just substituting a word. Any book you read is not solely the author’s words - it has had extensive input from an editor - so for those of us who are not published authors, AI can be our editors.

I think Ms. Stanger has identified the right boundaries and guardrails. The only point I might debate is “the structural diagnosis of a chapter that won’t cohere” - isn’t part of the process of “writing as thinking” to figure out the proper structure?

Think of it…if everybody used AI in the way they write, it could be hard to detect any plagiarism. How can you accuse someone of copying from someone else if they’re all using AI? How can you defend you own original works as being original and unique if others seem to write the same way you do, word for word, if we all use AI?

articles.title: Universities Should Prove They’re Playing Fair

comments.name: Jerome Abernathy
comments.body: Tests scores are a filter, not a ranking mechanism.  Above a fairly low cutoff, everyone can do the work.  Just as important are character traits like grit, empathy, and curiosity.

comments.name: Robert Cooper
comments.body:
DEI = Didn't Earn It

comments.name: David O
comments.body:
So out of a sample of 23, in 43% of the cases the average MMCAT score of rejected Asian or white applicants did not exceed the average MCAT score of accepted black applicants? Is that meager sample and narrow result the sole basis for Do No Harm's broad DEI accusation? Or is there also unsubstantiated suspicion that the non-responding schools had even higher white and Asian rejection rates?

Are test scores now the sole measure of a candidate's acceptability?

What was the score gap between each group? Was it minuscule or gaping?

What would the acceptance rates have been for Asian, white, and black applicants been had the MCAT scores been the sole criteria?

Do universities no longer have discretion in who they admit? By what criteria would classes admitted by test result only be superior to the actual classes the universities accepted?

Given the Duke's rush to condemn three white boys in the Lacrosse team rape hoax and their subsequent arrogance in defending their position, I would not be surprised by any suspicion of that faculty's integrity. But absent answers to the above questions, one should suspect that Do No Harm may have its own racial agenda and is not living up to its name.

The nuclear family runs on anarcho-communism; from each according to his ability (mom & dad) to each according to his needs (minor children). 

We don't expect infants to do anything but receive. As they grow to toddlerhood and beyond, they gradually take on age-appropriate responsibilities and contribute, but until emancipation, mom & dad are accountable.

This does not scale because the nuclear family (and certain familial extensions) is constrained by bonds of love and blood. Hence attempts at scale end in massive government debt or worse - massive government control and the Gulag Archipelago.

When colleges return their children to the embrace of anarcho-communism instead of boosting their emancipation, they turn them into individuals incompatible with the real world.

And that assumes the parents truly worked to enforce age-appropriate responsibilities and contributions. Too many moder horror stories of parents who did not...

comments.name: chris bullard
comments.body:
History shows fringe groups succeed only when leveraging deep structural crises or capturing mass popular alignment.

The DSA is a fringe group.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), represents less than 0.1% of the U.S. electorate and operates within a heavily entrenched two-party duopoly protected by multi-billion-dollar campaign apparatuses.

Unlike historical movements that overthrew regimes, the DSA functions primarily inside a mainstream capitalist party, where its policy aims are continually diluted by the center-left majority.

Furthermore, public polling consistently demonstrates that broad majorities of Americans favor regulated capitalism over socialism, neutralizing radical systemic transformation.

Thus, institutional guardrails and ideological resistance render the DSA a localized pressure group, not an existential threat to the status quo.

Nobody is coming for your capitalism or the free market system.

What Trump is coming for is your vote. Pulitzer Prize-winning authoritarian expert Anne Applebaum, author of Autocracy Inc., herself a former conservative, warns Trump's GOP is following the identical playbook used to end democracy in Hungary and Venezuela, engineering elections you can never win.

Republicans had a choice between a functioning government or corruption and chaos, they chose corruption and chaos.

Stop protecting a malignant narcissistic demagogue, Trump, and start supporting America.

Dump Trump in the mid-terms, then impeach.

Most people recognize the music of The Phantom but not many can sing along with it.  There is something about the plaintive score and stirring story of injustice that people love. But I had noticed that, in India, the old Hindu traditions of learning for its own sake -- because learning is one of the accepted paths (marg) to enlightenment -- was still a legitimate answer to questions of employment, which were raised then as they are now. Gyana-yoga is one of the paths taught by Sri Krishna to Arjuna in the "Bhagavadgita," and it is today carried out in other private universities, like Shanti-Vedanta, founded by Sri  Aurobindo, and Sayajirao University in Vadodara. Indians confront learning differently from Americans, because they have traditions that go back thousands of years, when associations of gurus and chelas dotted the forests during the "brahmacharya" life stage. Perhaps there is need to remember such traditions.

I was living in India when thousands of Chinese and Tibetans fled from the rushing Mao armies into Kolkata and the northern Himalayas. Many of my friends fled also from Burma and settled in India. I was living in the Darjeeling area, and I remember hastily packing a trunk of books and notes and shipping it to Mumbai, as far as possible from the threatened Chinese invasion -- which didn't materialize, just a few skirmishes. But we all, who were teaching in the various hill schools, were assigned to groups of children to flee, if necessary, through the steep mountains into the distant plains where the Himalayas ended -- a desperate escape that fortunately we didn't have to implement, because the Gurkha Division of the Indian army managed to contain the Chinese troops, though many of them perished. There's not a state in this country, probably not even a county in this country that doesn't have some representation of a cuisine born elsewhere then brought here. And we're finally getting examples of the food that existed here on this land before this country was even a dream. Not every place is as excellent as Yerord Mas, of course, but that doesn't detract from the sheer abundance of variety. All of this, all of this pleasure we derive from elsewhere, and yet, as a country--because of the powers that be (not every individual needless to say)--we are retrenching, pulling away from the rest of the world, thumbing our nose at it. If only we could be guided by the grand global community of food, instead of all the other things that propel politics. We need places like Yerord Mas and people like Mr. Grigoryan. We need more and more. We need to sit down at the table with the rest of the world. Not just for dinner now and again, but for every meal. Expanding our food horizons should help us expand all our horizons. Unfortunately, it doesn't enough yet. Maybe that's because too many (we all know of some) who are wedded to the corporate food that the US exports and are blind to the joys of bringing goods and traditions and people from elsewhere  into this country. I wish we would learn! Maybe Yerord Mas will help.

I was a graduate student at Texas Tech in the 1990s and taking a Victorian literature course. The instructor was a conservative Christian deacon who took a casual poll during class, based on a document that I suspect was from the Heritage Foundation or other Republican think tank. The questions concerned a return to "the classics," the traditional literary canon during a time when postmodern critical approaches were on the rise. Most in class saw the benefit of studying the canon. I myself wrote a masters thesis on the English Puritan Commonwealth and its influence on Daniel Defoe, but I did frame the study using postmodern approaches. There are benefits in balancing the postmodern and the traditional.

But Creighton's ideology about sexuality and gender simply defies science. This is enormously troubling. Literature reflects the times, and if authors are addressing sexuality and gender in fiction and factually-based writings, this benefits society. It's distressing to see faculty flee TTU; but it's inevitable if Trumpy restrictions hamper freethought. imagination, and honest research that is peer-reviewed.

comments.name: C In NY
comments.body:
Data centers should be required to provide their own electricity rather than shifting the cost of their enormous power demands onto the existing electrical grid. When a data center creates a massive new demand for electricity, utilities must invest in additional generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure—and those costs are ultimately borne by all ratepayers. Residential customers should not be forced to subsidize highly profitable data centers through higher electric bills. If these facilities need extraordinary amounts of power, they should be responsible for providing and paying for the additional generation and infrastructure required to serve them.

No data center should be approved unless it shows how it can provide its own power and cooling.
